Short title.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I desire to move, seconded by Mr. McMillan:
That the bill be amended by inserting the following therein as section 3 of the bill and renumbering section 3 as section 4:
3. Upon	receipt	by Secretary	of	State	of
Canada of a duly certified copy of an order in council passed by the lieutenant governor in council of the province of Ontario-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is a political fol-de-rol.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will read it
again:
That the bill be amended by inserting the following therein as section 3 of the bill, and renumbering section 3 as section 4:
3. Upon	receipt	by Secretary	of	State	ofCanada of a duly	certified copy	of	an orderin council passed by the lieutenant governor in council of the province of Ontario requesting that this act be brought into force in that province, the governor in council	may,	by
proclamation, declare that this act shall come into force on a day to be named in the said proclamation, not less than three months after the date of the receipt of such request by the Secretary of State.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We should understand the meaning of this amendment, as it places
within the discretion of this government the decision whether or not this measure shall be brought into effect. The province of Ontario could consent to the mode or the manner provided by this amendment, and then the governor in council of Canada would have the option of deciding at his own discretion whether or not by proclamation the bill should be brought into force and effect. If I understand this amendment correctly, unless the governor in council brings this bill into force and effect within -a certain time it remains null and void for all time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I absolutely-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have not yet explained the amendment. The main objection of the Ontario members who oppose this bill is that a divorce court is being forced upon Ontario. The result of this amendment would be that such a court would not be forced upon Ontario unless they asked for it, and until they passed legislation which would enable them to do so. There is nothing new about this amendment, because I drew it up in 1928 when I first agreed to sponsor a divorce bill. In the few remarks I made a week or two ago I mentioned that these amendments would be offered when the bill came up for second reading. It is not, as an hon. gentleman has said, political propaganda; it is simply a desire to satisfy those Ontario members who have opposed the measure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Why do you not try to
satisfy those in favour of it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am absolutely opposed to this amendment. In the first place, I do not believe that the parliament of Canada has any jurisdiction to give effect to such an amendment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has sat silent and listened to this proposal made by one of his supporters, a proposal which suggests that legislation passed by this house shall be subject to a decision of the provincial legislature in Toronto-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And he would not give
a nickel to that province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: -a Tory government to whom, it has been suggested, the Prime Minister would not give a thing. He would not recognize the government of the province of Ontario when it comes to a nickel, yet when it comes to deciding-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order.
Divorce Court for Ontario

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-this very important
question of divorce-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. members do
not like that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-the Prime Minister
has not one word to say.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is simply passing
the buck.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is no question
but that the proposal of the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Smith) is unconstitutional. There are hon. members in this house who have a realization of the duty which they have to perform, and they are not willing to take dictation in regard to this matter from any province, even the province of Ontario where good government prevails. I for one am not prepared to surrender the right of deciding by my vote in this house what shall be done in regard to this question of divorce. Let me emphasize that I am as much opposed as any hon. member in this house to the easier granting of divorces, but I realize that this question has been treated by the house almost with ridicule. We have seen the travesty of the granting of divorces by this house. This is not a question of the merits of divorce

I address my remarks to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)-it is not a question of whether it is right or wrong, but rather a question of the method, of the plan, and of what shall be done with these cases. Even those hon. members who are opposed to divorce must realize that the present method pf granting these decrees is nothing less than a joke, if I may be pardoned for using that word. We ask that this question be considered under the same terms as is a question of right or wrong, or a question of justice as between man and man-before the courts. I object to an amendment being introduced which is absolutely contrary to the rules of this parliament. The amendment means that those of us who come from the province of Ontario are being asked to surrender our right to pronounce upon this matter. Others from Ontario may be willing to surrender that right, but we will not consent to our privileges as members of this parliament being usurped by an amendment framed to meet the approval of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel it
to be my duty to oppose this amendment. If there is one thing which has been made clear by the discussion upon this question, it is the fact that divorce has been committed to this parliament. In passing this bill through its

second reading we have decided the principle that divorces should be handled by the Courts of Ontario.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: As delegated by this parliament.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: As delegated by this parliament. I agree absolutely with the reported statement of the premier of Ontario as it came to us in that circular from the Anglican council, that it is not his business at the present time to interfere in this matter. As has been made abundantly clear, the duty has been delegated to us. It has been said in some quarters that we are forcing this upon Ontario against the wishes of the people of that province. Even supposing that were true, we are still doing it in the exercise of our proper functions as members of the parliament of Canada. I do not think there can be any doubt upon that point. But are we forcing it upon Ontario in opposition to the majority of the members from that province? It would be very interesting to look at the vote as it was recorded the other night. We voted on an amendment. That amendment was defeated by a majority of thirteen. Then we voted on the second reading of the bill and that motion was carried by a majority of thirteen. If you look over the vote, and if I have not made a mistake, the number of members from Ontario who voted in favour of that bill was just thirteen more than the number who voted against it, so that practically speaking we can count out all the other members who voted and say that the majority of the members from Ontario have decided in favour of the bill. I feel very strongly on this matter and I shall conceive it my duty to vote against the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This bill proposes to vest in the provincial courts of Ontario certain jurisdiction with respeet to the adjudication of matters which are at present in the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. Parliament has the right to do this; it has the right to impose on provincial courts duties in federal matters. There was a time when the right of the federal parliament to do this was discussed and challenged, and the matter was submitted to the courts; but since the decision of the privy council in the case of Valin vs. Langlois with regard to controverted elections in Montmorency, it is generally accepted that parliament has the right to take such action. Such is not the case, for instance, in the United States, where congress has no right to impose burdens or duties on state courts, but in Canada I claim that we have that right. In doing so, however, I think to some extent we

Divorce Court for Ontario
are interfering, though we have the right to do so, with the administration of justice in the provinces, especially in a case like this when it has been represented to us in the house that we are forcing a divorce court upon a province the majority of the people of which are opposed to such a step being taken.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I say that it has been
represented to us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The only way to know is
by what this house says.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not sure about that.
I have heard the hon. member for South Huron on this side and the hon. member for North Huron on the other side say that they cannot find in their constituencies anybody who is in favour of such a court. Surely the expression of views of these two members is entitled to consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: They can vote against the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it not a good move on the part of the hon. member for Stormont to provide that before this legislation comes into force, the province of Ontario should in some way express its views with regard to the matter?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It has done so through its members here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I remember my hon.
friend was not so keen in saying that the province had pronounced on the question when on the first vote the majority of the Ontario members voted against the bill. I did not hear my hon. friend say that the province had expressed its views at that time. This is a matter regarding a moral issue, something which goes deep into the hearts and souls of the people. It is a big social, moral and religious issue in the opinion of many people in that province. Why not, before this legislation comes into force, have the province of Ontario express its views through its leading representatives provimcially, because we are enacting a law not for the whole of Canada but for Ontario alone.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: What about Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
An hon. member spoke about Quebec a few minutes ago. We do not want this to be forced upon Quebec any more than we want it to be forced on Ontario. It is because I would not want a similar law to be forced upon an unwilling province such as Quebec which will never agree to this law, that I do not want it to be forced upon
Ontario in the same way. What is the harm in this amendment? As I said, this is a moral issue, and after all there are precedents along the same lines in the statutes of Canada. There is the Canada Temperance Act, for instance. The probihition of importation of liquor is a federal matter entirely, but we have placed in the statute books a law stating that we will prohibit imports of liquor into any province only after that province, by order in council furnished to the Secretary of State of Canada, has expressed a willingness that we should do so. The Juvenile Delinquents Act is another statute which deals with a social policy, and there again the act comes into force in any province only after an order in council has been passed by the provincial authorities asking us to put it into force. In the Lord's Day Act, another measure dealing with a moral and social question, parliament has enacted a law, but it has taken good care to say that no prosecution shall be instituted except with the approval and consent of the attorney general of the province in which the prosecution is to be taken. There are many precedents for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Stormont. I do not like the amendment; I do not like the bill; I am opposed to the principle of the bill, but I say at least we should accept the amendment and not force this measure upon an unwilling province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am opposed to the bill, and I am also opposed to the amendment. The question of marriage and divorce is under the jurisdiction of parliament; we shall have to assume the responsibility .in the matter and I am not going to try to evade that responsibility. I will not agree to subordinating the jurisdiction of parliament to that of any of our provincial legislatures. I am satisfied that I am right when I say that every matter within the jurisdiction of this parliament can properly be determined by the members here, and that they for all federal purposes represent in this house every province in the Dominion. We have the responsibility. It looks as if this bill would carry. AVell, then, let us stand up and vote according to what we think right in the matter. Do not get out from under; stand up and vote according to your conscience. Do not pass the responsibility on to a body that has no responsibility to us in the matter at all. This parliament has the jurisdiction. Now let it act. I am heartily against the bill and heartily against the amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I feel with the Minister
of Justice and my hon. friend from South
Divorce Court for Ontario

Wellington that this bill is within the competence of the federal parliament. Where was the mover of this amendment, my hon. friend from Stormont, last year? What was the gist of his motion last year? And in connection with the withdrawal of that motion at that time, what was the statement of the Prime Minister? That he at this session would introduce a measure which would take this question out of politics. Where is the Prime Minister to-day? He was absent when two or three votes on this question were being taken; whether intentionally or not, I would not be harsh enough to say, but nevertheless when the final bell rang he gave a vote for the bill on the condition that an amendment would be made to it that it should not come into force until the government of the province of Ontario had requested it. Why should he pass the buck to the province of Ontario? If he is in favour of this bill, why not be manly and bold enough to come out and say so openly? The province of Ontario does not desire this measure. It is being forced on the province of Ontario by those who are not residents of Ontario, by members of this house from outside Ontario-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And members
for Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are endeavouring
to force this bill on the province. The bill was killed once, but they have brought it back again, and to-night we are dealing with the remains. For my part I refuse to vote either for the bill or for the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Stormont, because I believe the amendment is simply passing the buck. It is insincere, and is moved purely for political purposes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am utterly opposed to
the principle of divorce. I am opposed to the bill, and I am opposed to the amendment of the hon. member for Stormont. The Prime Minister of this country last year when this legislation was before the house gave a solemn pledge and promise to the members of this house and to the country that at this session of parliament he would introduce legislation to deal with this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Instead of that, for some
reason best known to himself, he has seen fit only to vote a couple of times on this bill, although he gave a solemn promise that he would deal with the matter this year in the house. He gave that promise to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but to this day he has not seen fit to come forward

and tell the house just exactly what he intends to do or what he wants to do on this question. I believe that the present amendment is simply an effort on/ the part of the government to sidestep its duties and1 responsibilities with regard to this whole question of divorce. It is the same old trick of trying to sidestep the issue and shelve off the responsibility on some other person, instead of facing the issue fairly and squarely here. The province of Ontario has never asked for divorce courts that I am aware of. There is not a citizen in the constituency I have the honour to represent who has ever asked that Ontario shall have a divorce court, and as long as I am in this house I am prepared to support the views of the constituency that I have the honour to represent, whether my constituents be Liberal or Conservative. I do not happen to be in the position of the Prime Minister, who does not care a five-cent piece if they happen to be Conservative. It is my intention to face this issue squarely and to vote for both Liberals and Conservatives in my constituency, who I believe are opposed to the principle of the bill itself and to this shelving proposition of the hon. member for Stormont.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think I need
reiterate my views on this question; for ten years I have voted and spoken in the same way with regard to it. I agree with the hon. member for North Renfrew when he says that this measure is being forced upon the province of Ontario by people who are living outside the province. There are not enough votes in this house from the province of Ontario to carry the measure. I protest against its being forced on the province by people living outside, and I will continue to protest against such a course. I do think that there ought to be a spirit of sportsmanship in this house and that when a minority is defeated it ought to give in to the majority. For ten years, I say, I have apposed such a measure as this. For the first time we are beaten. The bill has been given its second reading by a majority of the house, even if members from the province of Ontario have also voted for it. I feel that the amendment of the hon. member for Stormont is nothing but a piece of subterfuge whereby hon. members can get under the table and shirk their responsibility, play more or less the parts of cowards, and not come out and register their votes as they ought to register them either for or against this measure. What is to be gained by this? We have heard from the premier of Ontario that he will1 not ask for a divorce court; then I ask those who are

Divorce Court for Ontario
attempting to force the measure upon the province, what is there to be gained by carrying an amendment which means nothing? In my parliamentary career, Mr. Chairman, I have never yet reached that stage where I would be a party to killing my own bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Carried.

speechtext: Who said earried?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Go ahead, doctor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman,
we have reached the stage where we ought to consider the position of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is the leader of the government. A year ago he gave his promise to the house that he would offer a solution of this question. Now I ask him and I ask the house: Have we not, as members, a right to know what his solution is? I admit it is a troublesome question to some of us who do not believe in divorce. It is probably a still more troublesome question to members of the government who draw their support solidly from one province which is so absolutely opposed to divorce. maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I made a statement at the last session of parliament m which I set out the particulars of the arrangement. It was thought desirable that the statement should be made to parliament in that form. The record appears in Hansard; the statement was made intentionally in that form. One of the important features of the immigration arrangement between Japan and Canada is that passports must be signed or vised by designated officials. The viseing of passports for Japanese coming to Canada is part of the function of the legation, in many instances it may involve in advance the searching of individual records and the ascertaining of specific facts and information. As hon. members know, an important conference has been recently held in the Orient dealing with Pacific relations. Canada was represented at that conference by some of her best known citizens. I believe those who represented Canada found the presence of a legation in Tokyo extremely helpful. They found that the legation placed them in a position where they could very quickly become acquainted with those matters which from a Canadian point of view deserved careful consideration. The minister has very wisely sought to familiarize himself with political and economic conditions in Japan before attempting other duties, and his time up to the present has been devoted to the establishment of the legation on the right principles and in accordance with correct methods of procedure. From time to time special questions may come up, and as they do they will be dealt with individually. I do not know that it is possible to state a policy for Canada with respect to the Orient other than that of seeking in every particular to maintain the most friendly relations with the peoples of that portion of the world. It is the duty of the legation to see that no problem arises as between Japan and ourselves which through diplomatic handling can be prevented. With relation to problems which concern countries other than Canada and Japan, problems which have an imperial significance-if we wish to use that phrase-or a world significance, I would say that the relation of the Canadian minister in Japan to the British ambassador would be the same as the relation of Canada's minister at Washington to the British ambassador in that city. We have been told repeatedly by
Sir Esme Howard, former British ambassador at Washington, that he found the establishment of the Canadian legation there, and in particular the presence of Hon. Mr. Massey, of the utmost assistance. He believes that the whole British relationship has been materially strengthened as a result of Canada having opened a legation in Washington and through the helpful cooperation there has been between the Canadian minister and the British ambassador. I believe the same will prove to be equally true in Tokyo.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the Orient covers a lot of ground. The relations between Japan and China are a factor in questions which may arise even as between Japan and this country. I may say that when Sir Austen Chamberlain, at the time Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, was in this city and we were discussing the question of the opening of a legation in Tokyo, he expressed to me the view that in his opinion it would be very helpful to the Canadian minister at Tokyo to visit China, and he stated that in the event of that course being thought desirable the British government would facilitate the movements of the Canadian minister in every way possible. At the time it seemed to me the idea was a good one, and it has been acted upon to a certain extent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

tical side, he is enabled to obtain access to governmental departments that a mere trade commissioner could not so speedily secure. From what I have read of the operations of our present minister at Tokyo since he went there, I should judge that his time has been principally taken up in the promotion of trade, and that in promoting trade his one service is that by virtue of the dignity which attaches to the position he is given t'he right of access to officials who would be denied to one engaged as a representative of trade only, and the minister thereby has extended the sphere of influence of Canadian exporters. So far as I can find out that seems to be a fair statement of the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has stated the position as it is at present very fairly, although I should not restrict the minister's functions and services as much as he has done. The presence of the minister in Tokyo, perhaps more than anything else, has brought this country to the attention of the government, the large financial and commercial interests, and the people of Japan. That is a phase of our representation in the Orient which I think is quite important. I believe it is true that the presence of the minister in Japan has made it possible for numbers of persons in this country to become acquainted with individuals and firms in Japan by correspondence and in other ways and with opportunities so far as furthering Canada's interest in the Orient is concerned, which otherwise would not have been possible.
With respect to the establishment, the personnel consists of the minister, the Hon. Herbert Marler and a secretariat of three. Mr. Langley is the first secretary, and he is also the representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Mr. H. L. Keenleyside, is also a first secretary, and Mr. K. P. Kirkwood is third secretary. There is a clerical staff of three stenographers; there is a Japanese translator and an assistant; a Japanese stenographer and a messenger and office boy, who I imagine are also Japanese.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: This is the Canadian office at Geneva, which has been in existence for some years. An increase of $2,500 has been necessitated by additional clerical work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The nomenclature of the vote seems to have been altered each year.
I have 'been trying to check up the votes for the last three or four years for the League of Nations, and I find this year that vote No. 243 covers the salaries and expenses of the office of the Canadian advisory officer; vote No. 244 covers Canada's contribution to the expenses of the League of Nations; vote No. 245 covers the expenses of Canadian delegates to the assembly, council and com-

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
missions of the League of Nations, and vote No. 246 covers the publications of the League of Nations. The total of those votes amounts to something over $233,000. In making a rough check of the votes for previous years,
I find the vote for salaries and expenses to be roughly as follows:
1927	 $10,000
1928	 12,000
1929		 21,000
1930		 22,500
1931		 25,000
Although I have made this computation very hurriedly, I think it is correct. It shows that from 1921 to 1931 there has been an increase from $10,000 to $25,000. The same thing is true with regard to the vote for the League of Nations, that vote having increased from $150,000 for 1927 to 1184,000 for this year. It would appear that the votes are being increased each year, and as a member of this house I would like to know why. I cannot see why this vote should be increased over last year, and I would like to have an explanation from the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The question
of my hon. friend will be best answered perhaps by my reading a paragraph from the report of the Department of External Affairs. This paragraph will indicate how the work of the Canadian advisory office at Geneva has been increased. It reads:
The work of the Canadian Advisory Office at Geneva as the established channel of communication between the government of Canada and the League of Nations, has continued to grow with the development of the league's activities and the responsibilities involved in the place in the league's organizations which has been attained by the Dominion. As a temporary member of the council and as a member of the governing body of the International Labour Office, Canada is called upon to participate in all the important conferences and administrative activities of the league. In addition to assisting at meetings of the council and of the assembly, the Canadian Advisory Officer has represented Canada in the meetings of the preparatory disarmament commission, the conference on revision of the Red Cross convention, commissions for the preparation of the convention on private manufacture and supervision ' of manufacture of arms, and the conference for the suppression of counterfeiting. The advisory officer represented the Minister of Labour at the sessions of the governing body of the International Labour Office and acted as a delegate at the sessions of the International Labour Conference. Reports on the various questions before the league have been forwarded and an increasing measure of information as to league activities furnished Canadian correspondents and the growing number of Canadians who visit Geneva.
As is shown by the paragraph which I have just quoted, Canada's representation at Geneva 2410-88
has become quite as important as that of any other country. Adequate representation has necessitated some slight additional expenditure. The division of the items is made simply to enable members of this house to estimate better what the activities are of the particular officers, and the work to which parliament is being asked to appropriate moneys.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not claim particularly that there is too much being spent, but it does strike me as strange that every time we open up an office of any kind-the Prime Minister has had a longer experience in civil service affairs than I have-whether it be in Canada, Geneva, Washington or elsewhere, the expenses of such office keep on increasing. Geneva is a considerable distance from Canada, and I would suggest that it might be well for the government, whether it is this government or the one which will succeed it, to check up the expenses of offices such as this. In reading the newspapers of England, the United States and Canada, I have seen protests against the expenses of the League of Nations. Most of those complaints were upon the ground that an immense civil service organization was being built up without any control being exercised. Considering the distance Geneva is from Canada, it is very easy to add a few extra clerks, secretaries and other assistants to the personnel, and hire a few extra automobiles without any check-up being made. Perhaps it is our duty to pay, but we should not permit the building up of such organizations without some check-up being made.
A hurried estimate of the expenditure for last year shows that they amounted to $215,000 for the Geneva vote, while the total for this year amounts to $233,000. I am quite certain that an examination of the votes for previous years will show that they have increased as the years went by. I suggest to the right hon. Prime Minister that the office at Geneva be informed that the people of Canada feel that unless it is absolutely necessary we should not have to go on increasing year by year the amount of money voted for that office. To a large extent this is true also with regard to the offices at Tokyo, Washington and other places. The sooner these outside offices are informed that this parliament is checking their expenses-at least in a general way; it would be very difficult to check them in detail-the better it will be for Canada as well as for the offices concerned. I for one desire to put myself on record as being opposed to this continual increase in the cost of running these offices, because after all the people have to pay the bills. A check-up of the civil service

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
in Canada will show that there is a continual growth from year to year, and the expenses of that growth are sufficient without a continual increase in the cost of a little civil service outside of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The votes with respect to Geneva are the same this year as they were last year, with the exception of the vote covering the salaries and expenses of the office, of the Canadian advisory officer, which vote has been increased by 82,500, to cover the additional clerk which I have already mentioned, and the vote covering Canada's contribution to the expenses of the League of Nations, which has been increased by 812,445.80. That is an increase, however, which we are not in a position to control. Our percentage of the expenditure of the League of Nations is something like per cent, and there has been an increase in the total expenses of the league due to certain new activities in which the league has become interested. There is, for example, an inquiry into certain diseases in Latin-American countries, the carrying out of the recommendations of the economic conference of 1927, conference on the codification of international law, the strengthening of the narcotic law, and in addition there is the contribution which the different countries are making to new buildings for the League of Nations. All of that accounts for part of the increase in the amount, but it is a division of the total expenses of the league which is made by the League of Nations itself, and not an expenditure which we are in a position to control except to the extent to which we can make our voice heard for economy at the league itself. With respect to the voice of Canada in the matter of league expenditure, I think I can assure my hon. friend that it has been on the side of economy and not of extravagance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I quite agree that the
Prime Minister is right in saying that the large increase is due to Canada's contribution to the League of Nations, and to a certain extent his statement that we have not much control over that is also correct. But I repeat that I read some months ago that Prance was protesting against the continual increase in her expenditure in connection with the League of Nations. I do not think we need be too proud to take the same attitude, because the expense in connection with the item of which the Prime Minister spoke, over which in a sense we have no control, has increased from $150,000 in 1928 to 8184,000 three years later. The only way in which that expense can be [Mr. Manion.l
kept down for all countries is for Canada to take its attitude through its representatives at Geneva, just as France, England and other countries should take their attitude through their representatives at the same place. In these days of high expenditures, neither France, England nor any other country can afford to pay more than it has to; and of course that applies to Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
While I have always
been an advocate of economy, there is true economy and false economy. I think at an earlier stage in the session I gave the figures showing that the military expenditures of the countries of the world for one year would run the League of Nations for six hundred years. If we really want to save money I would suggest to the hon. member for Fort William that we can cut it off the estimates of the Department of National Defence and with good economy add it to the expenditure that is being made at Geneva. It was my great privilege to see something of the work that was being done by the Canadian office in Geneva last fall.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope that was not the
cause of the increased expense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope not. Before
dinner the hon. member for Toronto Northwest said that we had a whole army at Geneva. We have six Canadians in the Canadian office and I must admit that they are a host in themselves. Doctor Riddell, the head of the office, Colonel Georges Vanier and Mr. E. D. McGreer were, I thought, about as fine types of Canadians as could be found anywhere and they were doing serious work for Canada. What is more, they were doing it enthusiastically, and this cannot always be said of members of the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let the hon. member speak for herself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not the least enthusiastic member of the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: How could they be anything else to the hon. member?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The office that we have at Geneva is really very beautiful, but it is not expensive, because thinking it was so beautiful I expected it would be expensive, so I asked what the rent was and I found it was amazingly low. I spent a good deal of time in the office with the three young women and the men I mentioned. I felt they were trying their very best to hold down expenses and spending only what money needed to be spent to do good work for Canada in Geneva.

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
I feel also that countries that have offices at Geneva are in a much better position while the assembly is in session than countries that do not have offices there. I am not trying to assist the Minister of External Affairs, but it seems quite reasonable that the expenditures would increase while we have a seat on the council of the League of Nations. I do not care to say anything more under this particular item, except this: let us not start economy on the peace end of our activities; let us begin to economize when the estimates of the Department of National Defence come up and then I will enlist the services of my good friend the hon. member for Fort William.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend probably
thinks we should cut down the navy too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will vote with her to
cut down the navy. I do not wish to be misunderstood as opposing our contribution to the League of Nations. I still take my attitude, with all due deference to the lady who has just taken her seat, that we might just as well be as economical as we can at Geneva and be as economical as we can at home. I did not have the advantage she had of visiting those offices or I might be defending the Prime Minister in this matter too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That may come also.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not wish to be in the position of always criticizing the League of Nations, but I should like to find out something about it. Who compose the league? What does it do? What are its functions? Wbo are Canada's delegates? There is a
labour delegation that goes over there and there are ladies going over there. Mrs. Mary Ellen Smith, who was supposed to be an impartial representative, went over there and when she came back she toured Canada addressing Liberal associations and criticizing the head of the party in this corner of the house. I am becoming alarmed at these expenditures. Canada is contributing the largest amount per capita of any member of the league. The mother country last year paid $395,000 to the League of Nations. I quote this from the Mail and Empire of a despatch from London of the 22nd March:
It cost Great Britain $100,000 for the reestablishment of its embassy in Moscow, according to the civil estimates issued to-day. Other estimates dealing with foreign affairs showed that Britain's contribution to the League of Nations increased during the year from $355,000.to $395,000 annually, this country paying 10.65 per cent of the total league expenses, not, however, including the international labour organizations.
That is what the mother country is expending. Is this country increasing its expenditures? I think the amount is $284,000 when it is totalled up. This money is absolutely wasted. The government are busying themselves in every capital in Europe about foreign affairs and they cannot attend to their own home affairs. They are spending $450,000,000 in this parliament. Charity begins at home. A five cent policy is the cheap politics of the head of the Department of External Affairs towards his own people. He may read from Industry and Humanity all he likes, but charity begins at home. I want to read one or two paragraphs to show what actually goes on at the league on which we are spending so much money. I am quoting from the League of Nations, First Impressions, by George Bernard Shaw in the Empire Review. He thus describes his first visit to the league in 1928:
When my presence at Geneva during the annual assembly of the League of Nations was mentioned in the press, I received several letters, of which the following is a fair sample:
"I cannot help being rather surprised and shocked to read that you 'sit on the bench of mockers and hypocrites' .... In this country every little child knows that the League of Nations is only a bluff and nothing but an instrument for the policy of the allied forces .... I really am at a loss to understand why you don't feel your responsibility as a mental tutor of the world, when taking such a step as taking part in the comedy of Geneva, which is a tragedy for every country that does not find mercy in the eyes of the world's high C finance."
This letter is not a stateman's utterance. It is a crude expression of the popular impatience which sees no more in the league than an in-

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
strument for the instantaneous extirpation of war, and is ready to throw it on the scrap-heap the moment it becomes clear that no such operation is possible, and that the big powers have not, and never have had, any intention of relinquishing any jot of their sovereignty, or depending on any sort of strength and security other than military.
Roughly and generally it is a fact that the pacifist oratory at the assembly is Christmas card platitude at best and humbug at worst. The permanent departments of the league have to fight hard to defeat the frequent attempts to sabotage it by the big powers through their deciduous members.
Whilst I was there the press was keeping the public amused, not to say gulled, by gossip about the assembly meetings, at which nothing happens but pious speeches which might have been delivered fifty years ago.
We have two hardy perennials at the league, the leader of the Senate Hon. Raoul Dandurand, and Sir George Foster. They seem to be two souls with but a single thought, two hearts that beat as one as to the league. I have heard in this house some of our delegates talking about our maritime ports. When they go over to the league for a nice trip they do not leave our maritime ports. No, they sail on the George Washington and other fine steamers from the port of New York. That is how much these favourite statesmen care about our maritime ports. I quote again:
It was so impossible to listen to them, or to keep awake during the subsequent inevitable translations, that the audience had to be kept in its place by a regulation, physically enforced,-
I wish we had this regulation in this house. Mr. Shaw continues:
-that no visitor should be allowed to leave the ball except during the five minutes set apart for that purpose between speech and translation. Fortunately, the young ladies of the Secretariat, who have plenty of dramatic sense, arrange the platform in such a way that the president, the speakers, and the bureau are packed low down before a broad tableau curtain which, being in three pieces, provides most effective dramatic entrances right and left of the centre. When a young lady secretary has a new dress, or for any other reason feels that she is looking her best, she waits until the speaker

possibly a Chinese gentleman carefully plodding through a paper written in his best French has reduced half the public galleries to distraction and the other half to stertorous slumber, when she suddenly, but gracefully, snatches the curtains apart and stands revealed, a captivating mannequin, whilst she pretends to look round with a pair of sparkling eyes for her principal on the bureau. The effect is electric: the audience wakes up and passes with a flash trom listless desperation to tense fascination, to the great encouragement of the speaker who, with his back to the vision beautiful, fondly believes he has got them at last, nwfr. Ghumh 1
That is the kind of thing, cheap political vaudeville, that goes on at the League of Nations. We have been reading in the papers of a peace parley of five powers, but it is really six powers. Canada is represented there, this great nation with its wonderful fleet and its wonderful contribution to the league, the heaviest contribution of any country. Canada is represented at the peace parley by Colonel Ralston, the Minister of National Defence. He was wired to the other day to come home, but he did not come. He has asked to see the thing through. The Prime Minister of France, wdien asked by newspaper men why he was leaving the parley at London for Paris, said, "I cannot spend all day looking out of my hotel wdndow however fine the weather may be," and outside he asked the reporters for a cigarette. The United States report says he was tired of it, and it was reported that our representative was also getting tired of it. The net result should be that our Minister of National Defence should be asked to come home and allow the mother country to look after European affairs. What we should be doing is to attend to the functions of this parliament and be passing legislation for the benefit of the working classes of this country. Let us do something practical, but we spend more than half our time trying to prove that Canada is a nation and that the league is the cure for all the ills of the human race. Dear knows what our representative at, the peace parley is going to bring back in his club bag. The Minister of Justice brought back a wonderful new magna charts by which we were to be released from the tyranny forever of Downing street and have as an adviser a governor general who would make speeches just like a member of parliament does and cease being a governor, only a viceroy. The delegates to the league are all politicians. They are selected after the fashion of the Prime Minister when he is dealing with unemployment. He separates the sheep from the goats. No Tories are ever allowed to represent Canada at the league.
The first item under the heading of Geneva is for the salaries and expenses of the office of the Canadian Advisory Officer. He is a doctor, of what I don't know yet. Everybody connected with External Affairs is a doctor. What he is a doctor of I do not know. Some of the quack cures of these doctors on external affairs have been hurting this country and the British Empire. Who does the Canadian Advisory Officer advise? Does he advise parliament? A doctor advised the industrial and international relations committee to put up $600,000 to $1,000,000 for chairs in our universities to teach our young people something

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
about foreign affairs and to get the international formulae. I have one hundred and twenty-five students of Toronto universities that I am trying to get a job for now. Mr Cyrus Eaton, the great Cleveland financier and philanthropist, went to Cleveland in his student days at McMaster and stayed there when he graduated. He would not be one of those who would stay at home and imbibe this magnificent dream of our new status, this international diplomacy which everybody gets so fed up on. Every child in the schools is to be given a copy, if you please, so that he may learn what our magnificent diplomats are doing at the League of Nations. Our university students, over fifty per cent of them, go to the States and other foreign countries. We are thus exporting our greatest assets, our clever students.
I have asked who composes the league. We have had twelve years of nothing but peace pacts and agreements and speeches, and what has been the result? It has been the utter failure of open diplomacy, which Mr. Woodrow Wilson so strongly, and so disastrously for the peace of Europe, advocated. Will Italy have anything to do with the league? Mussolini calls it a lot of horse play; that is the phrase of the Prime Minister of Italy. Will Germany or Russia have anything to do with it? Russia is mobilizing millions of men and marching on China, equipped with tanks and all modern military equipment. I quote from the January, 1930, number of the English Review:
At present, while peace is chattered about in the suburbs of Western Europe, anarchy is spreading over vast tracts of territory. Millions of men are under arms; millions of homes are in constant peril of loot and desecration. Before 1914 these things would have roused the conscience of Europe. To-day Europe is so conscious of its moral superiority and unswerving devotion to peace that it will not move a finger. It will only sign pacts and pass resolutions. These war books reflect this evil mood. They are teaching people that all the good things in life come easily and automatically and that all the evil is due to the interference of politicians and soldiers with the peaceful evolution of society. That is a lie. One glance round the world to-day proves it so. But the literary coteries who are booming their books will not take that one glance. They must be taught to do so.
There are a whole lot of sensible people in this country who do not believe in the league, who have lost confidence in it. The league has been a nice, pleasant annual gathering, providing an enjoyable trip overseas on the most modern ships, sailing out of the port of New York instead of out of our St. Lawrence and maritime ports, for a lot of favourites of the government, and all the flatterers of the
government took passage. The boys have a nice pleasant trip and imbibe the higher statesmanship of Geneva and all its vanities. What do they do when they go over there? They run up a lot of bills and nobody knows what they are for. Where is the Auditor General, what is he doing about this particular department? Have you ever seen a statement of the expenses of this league? I have looked for such a statement in vain. Let me enumerate these expenses:
Canada's contribution to the expenses of the League of Nations for 1930, including secretariat, International Labour Organization and permanent court of international justice, $184,227.
A permanent court of international justice for what? To help pacify Europe? What we want in this country is a court of justice that will give the working class a chance in Canada, that will give them bread instead of a stone. Here is another item:
Expenses of Canadian delegates to the assembly, council and commissions of the League of Nations, $21,000.
Who are these delegates? What political party do they belong to? Are they supporters of the government? Of course they are; that is the reason they get the trip. Then we have these expenses for publications:
Publications of League of Nations for distribution to members of parliament and a grant to the League of Nations Society in Canada, $3,000.
That is $3,000 thrown away. The whole vote of about $243,000 is money that might be spent to much better purpose in giving relief to our women and children suffering in the cities and towns of this country- This expenditure would not be so bad if it was helping remove the risk of war, but the Prime Minister of France says that that risk is just as great as it ever was. The amount of money this league is spending is going up by leaps and bounds. This afternoon I was referring to the ultimate disunion of the empire as the outcome of the policy of this government. To-day in Washington there is the representative of the Irish Free State and our own representative. Not only is this government interfering in Europe, it is interfering in the Pacific too.
But to return to Europe. It is only about a week ago that the Prime Minister laid on the table Senator Dandurand's declaration with respect to the optional clause. He said it could be put down on a foolscap sheet of paper. It should have been made on April Fool's day. Senator Dandurand holds up his right hand and makes that declaration in relation to the optional clause. If Canada
1390	COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
got out of Europe altogether and our government contented itself with trying to govern Canada instead of Europe, this country would be far better governed than it is to-day. There are a few matters on the front page of today's paper that might well engage the attention of this particular department; one being the dismissal of British subjects from their jobs in the United States. Why has not that been brought to the attention of the League of Nations? The American people do not belong to the league. They started the league and then they said they would not have anything to do with it. Now they are going to build a canal of their own down through New York state, and there will be no deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway owing to the way Canada has run away from the St. Lawrence. What is the government doing about that? Would it not be better for our representative in Washington to get busy about something practical? These leagues never were of much use. After the great Napoleonic wars ending in 1815 the Holy Alliance was formed by the emperors of Austria and Russia and the king of Prussia, but it came to nothing. The United States covenanted to protect Belgium, but they did not do anything to carry out that covenant. The Persians, the Greeks and the Romans all had leagues, but to no purpose. I have never yet heard of a league that did anything to justify its existence. I fail to see what benefit the government is getting from this expenditure. The League of Nations has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. If we spent one half of the time on the economic problems confronting this country that is spent on this League of Nations- if Canada would only mind her own business and keep out of Europe, it would be far better for the Dominion and the empire. When Laurier took office our national expenditure was $36,000,000; to-day it is about $450,000,-000-roughly half a billion dollars, although our population is very little more than we had in 1896. The government is simply spending money like water. It would be much better if they spent this money in helping the motherland keetp up her navy. I venture to say that anybody who wants to be a delegate at Geneva had better get a promise from the government at once, because I believe the league will blow itself uip if you give it time. We are paying to become a nation. Here is a paragraph about the league from the Morning Post:
The anniversary of the Battle of Trafalgar yesterday serves as the peg on which the Morning Post to-days hangs its leading editorial on "Naval Necessities." Referring
rMr. Church.]
especially to Canada, the newspaper said: "Canada owes both her existence and her liberties in the first place to the Royal Navy, and then to that balance of power which maintains the British Empire in the new world as in the old. Let that balance be destroyed and how long, despite all pacts and treaties, would any part of that Empire rest secure?
"Canada is growing mightily, not only in industry and agriculture, but in commerce. Her ships are even now bringing to her people the fruits, sugar and other tropical commodities of the West Indies. For the protection of that traffic her naval provision of two destroyers is almost ludicrously inadequate. Her vast grain trade, her sea carriage east, west and south- these owe their security to the existence of the Royal Navy under whose benignant shade Canada has grown and prospered.
"These things are taken so much as a matter of course as to be ignored in the outlook of most of the Dominions. Yet it remains true that the trade of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have no other security than the fleet which they seldom see, but of which the very existence is a perpetual restraint to any potential enemy. The ideal of peace in an unarmed world is not served by ignoring the truth."
It would be far better for Canada if we devoted the money we are spending on the League of Nations as a contribution towards the British fleet. That is the only real League of Nations; all other leagues are mere moonshine. The British navy has been the only league thait has protected civilization and humanity for the past century. I am not going to move a reduction of the vote because I think it Should be out out altogether. I would give the League of Nations as much as the Prime Minister would give to unemployment-five cents; and that would be too much.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before the vote passes, Mr. Chairman, I have a suggestion to make to the Prime Minister. I think it is an opportune time to draw his attention to the fact that Greece is celebrating the hundredth anniversary of her independence, and Great Britain and the United States have sent their congratulations to that country. I would suggest that Canada might follow their example.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to offer a suggestion. It is only recently that we in Canada have been under the necessity of dealing with foreign affairs. So far there does not seem to be any machinery set up by which we can secure an intelligent discussion of these matters. We have no established procedure. It does seem to me that not merely should these items of expenditure in connection with the league be brought before the house but also the various policies that are being discussed in the league Should come under review. The other day in the

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
committee on industrial and international relations someone asked what we knew with regard to the rights of minorities. Senator Dandurand has been very active in regard to this matter and I fancy there is no country which takes a keener interest than we do in the rights of minorities. So far as I know, however, there has been no discussion in this house in regard to the matter, and no policy has been worked out. It may be that Senator Dandurand is working along the very best lines, but we have had no report other than what has been published in the records of the league. I submit to the Prime Minister there ought to be some very definite means adopted whereby consideration could be given to these affaire. We have set up a committee on industrial and international relations. It was on the suggestion of the Prime Minister that the second part was added and the committee given jurisdiction over international relations, but that phase of the work has never been taken seriously. This year for the first time a reference has been made to that committee, when it was asked to consider the motion of the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail). I do not know whether that committee as now constituted is the proper place to deal with external affairs or whether it might be desirable to have a separate committee. When there are so many matters of importance to be considered it might be well to have a separate committee. As we are aware, the United States senate oommittee on foreign affairs is very influential, and I can see no reason why we should not have a committee of that nature in connection with this house.
I hope the Prime Minister will understand that I am in sympathy with an extension of work along these lines, but I consider that we should have better opportunities of becoming informed, and we should have some voice in tiie determination of policies relating to external affairs.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before the item
carries I would like to have a statement from the Prime Minister. I wish to ask if we will have an opportunity at this session of the house to discuss Canada's foreign policies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not control either the procedure or the proceedings of the house. With the best of intentions I tried last session to meet my hon. friend on a difficult matter, but apparently I have not been able to accomplish my purpose either to his liking or to the liking of some other hon. members. I hesitate to promise anything which it may be impossible to fulfil. As far
as external affairs are concerned, the same opportunities are afforded for discussion of that subject as are afforded for the discussion of any other subject which may be considered by parliament. As to fixing a specific time I confess I find it somewhat difficult to undertake anything of that nature.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I suggest
to the Prime Minister that the question raised by my friend from Fort William (Mr. Man-ion) is worthy of the consideration of those who may represent Canada next year at the assembly? As the Prime Minister no doubt knows, there are half a dozen committees of the assembly, one of which deals with financial matters and the consideration of such questions as the division of expenses, what the total budget shall be, and things of that nature. It is very necessary that our representative on the financial committee should pay particular attention to the question that has been raised by the member for Fort William. The hon. member has said that there is a gradual increase from year to year in the expense of the league, and particularly in Canada's share of those expenses. I am of the opinion that the league is doing good work, but unless the matter is very carefully handled this country may be asked to pay more than its just share. In that connection I see no reason why the Prime Minister should not instruct our representative on the financial committee so that he may be able to consider the financial side of the question with greater care.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall be
only too ready to act on the suggestion of my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not very well satisfied with the situation as it has been left by the Prime Minister. In this item we have, for instance, grants made to the international labour office. I am keenly interested in what has been going on in connection with that office. There is no real opportunity under an item of this character to discuss in detail what the international labour office has been doing. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) is not present to-night and we are deprived of the information he could give us as to what has been done. He is not here to answer any questions or criticism that we may have to offer. I do not think anybody would suggest that this is a suitable opportunity to discuss matters of that kind. I do not want to be put in the position of having to move the adjournment of the house or to make a motion upon going into supply. I hope such procedure will not be necessary. I want it clear that I am
1392	COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
making no threat, but I do not think that a private member on this side of the house ought to be placed in the position where he has to move the adjournment of the house or make a motion upon going into supply before he can get consideration of matters of this kind. They are of sufficient importance to merit consideration by this house, and it is for that reason I appeal to the Prime Minister and ask that in some way they should be brought before the house. Would it not be possible to set aside a particular date for the discussion of league affairs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I point out to my hon. friend that about ten days have elapsed since I made the motion that the house go into supply to consider the estimates of the Department of External Affairs? As the hon. member knows, the consideration of the estimates is the opportune time to discuss any matter pertaining thereto. I deliberately brought on my estimates early in the session so that the fullest opportunity would be given to hon. members to discuss external affairs. In other years the criticism has been made that the estimates for this department have been considered at a time so late in the session that there was not opportunity for full discussion. This year they have been brought on at an early date, and for ten days past the house has been aware of the fact that these estimates would be considered just as soon as the house went into committee of supply. I cannot think of a better opportunity to discuss matters relating to the League of Nations than when the items in the estimates which affect the league are being considered. If my hon. friend can suggest a better opportunity that that afforded by supply, I would like to have his suggestion. It seems to me that supply affords the best of all opportunities. I may say that there will be two or three matters relating to League of Nations affairs which will come before the house shortly. There is one on the order paper at the present time relating to the optional clause. There are other matters, one of which relates to the approval of the protocol for the revision of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice, and another relating to the approval of the protocol for the accession of the United States to the protocol of signature of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice. These matters will afford opportunities for further discussions. I think the house will permit considerable latitude on any one of these subjects. There is no desire in any way to restrict consideration of these important matters.
[Mr. Woodsworth.l

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am considerably
troubled by these items we are voting for external affairs. I am convinced that we are paying more than any other nation receiving similar service. I think the figures for London, Washington, Paris, Tokyo and Geneva are much in excess of what the work could be done for. I do not think any other nation pays as much for the upkeep of any legation as we pay in the case of Washington, especially if we take into account the interest on the money we have invested there. It may be that the United States pays more with respect to Paris, but I should like to know if the Prime Minister can tell us of any nation which pays more for Tokyo than we pay. As far as Geneva is concerned it is proposed to expend this year about $235,000, and I do not believe we get value for it. It is not a question of "keeping up with the Joneses;" in these items we are running far ahead of them and setting a pace. Canada is the most extravagant of the nations with regard to its external affairs. When I think of the debate which just finished to-day; when I remember that we have no money for unemployment, it seems a shame. We have these sums of 8117,000, $100,000, 180,000, $233,000 and so on, but nothing for the unemployed. I want to ask the Prime Minister if something cannot be done, while he is at the head of the government, to economize in these matters. I know something about these trips abroad; at one time I crossed the ocean with some delegates who were going to attend the League of Nations, and they regarded it as a great joy trip.
I will tell you what I am satisfied I could do. I could take the sum of $50,000 and put a man in London who could take care of all Canadian interests there; for $25,000 I could put a man in Washington who would look after the situation there. You could allow the same sum for Paris and Tokyo, and it would be sufficient. If we were on the job; if we were desirous of advancing the interests of this country instead of being anxious to give people pleasant jobs and nice trips, we could take care of the financial interests, the foreign trade and the international relations of this country in a way that would benefit Canada, at a very much less cost than that which is now involved. It is appalling to me to see Canada paying these immense sums. If I am wrong I should like the Prime Minister to tell me what nations are paying more for similar services than we pay. There is no answer. I happen to know a gentleman who was recently appointed United States ambassador at Warsaw, and certainly in that

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
ease there was no appropriation like this. I remember that two years ago the complaint was made that we were trying to "keep up with the Joneses." I do not want anyone to outstep us in the race, but I object to our country setting the pace for all the others, and that is the position in which we are placing ourselves now in view of the amounts we are asked to vote for external affairs. I object, Mr. Chairman; we could do the business of the country more economically and more effectively at much less expense; at least that certainly is my opinion.
