speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Geneva-expenses of Canadian delegates to the assembly, council and commissions of the League of Nations, $21,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Just here I should like to say a word of commendation to the government for having placed the last delegation on what appears to me to be the proper footing; that is, the delegation was not composed entirely of supporters of the government. I believe Sir George Foster and Miss Macphail were members of that delegation, and they represent parties other than the Liberal party. We have a precedent for an action of that kind, since last year Lord Cecil was appointed a member of the British Empire delegation as representing the government of Great Britain. It strikes me that in these matters of such great interest to the country we should rise above narrow party lines. After all when it comes to matters of international importance we are all Canadians, and it seems to me the government should be commended for having taken action along this line.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
All prepared to take
trips together at the expense of the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, I do not think that is the idea; it seems to me this is a bigger thing than merely joy riding. I must confess that for a long time I was not tremendously enthusiastic about the league because it seemed to me simply a league of victors and was so circumscribed in its powers that it did not amount to a very great deal. However, as the years have gone by, within somewhat narrow limits, it is true, the league has done very good work, and as a matter of fact it is the only international organization in existence. I think any thoughtful student of world affairs must come to the conclusion that to-day we cannot go along just within our own national limits; we must have some form of world organization if we are to prevent world wars in the future.
Therefore I urge that we should support the League of Nations. If we recognize that Canada must play a part in the League of Nations, then we cannot talk in a cheap way about our delegates to that league taking a joy ride. One might just as well say that when we come to Ottawa to attend the sessions of this Dominion parliament and to look after the business of the country we are taking a joy ride. I think we must recognize that the league is coming to be something of a world parliament; we should choose our representatives just as carefully, and they should take their duties just as seriously, as is the case with representatives in our own legislative bodies. Our delegates have been in attendance at the league; they have come in contact with some of the world leaders and discussed some of the world problems, but there is no opportunity for them to present anything in the shape of a report to other members who have not had the opportunity of going to Geneva. Again I do not know just how this could be done. Some of us have discussed matters with them privately with a view to getting information. I do not suggest that most of us have anything to contribute, but rather that we should receive information as to what is going on, and then possibly have a chance to pass judgment on the policies which have been brought forward.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Since the matter has
been brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I want to say something about my appreciation of the action of the government in sending a parliamentary delegation to the League of Nations last September. I feel slightly embarrased in doing so, because I was one of the group sent. I did not accept the offer of the government as meaning that I would be given a joy ride. That it would be an excursion which would afford me pleasure was of course the case, but that was not the reason I accepted the offer. Hon. members will recall that last year I made the suggestion that the delegation sent to the meeting of the league should be non-partisan. The government acted upon my suggestion with alacrity, and I was taken more or less by surprise as the government does not often take my suggestions seriously. Sir George Foster was appointed to go, not because he was a Conservative, I take it, but because he had done very excellent work for peace and for the League of Nations. I was asked to go, possibly because I had been interested in this subject-I hope that was the reason. When Sir George Foster, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott), the Minister of

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
National Revenue (Mr. Euler), Senator Dandurand and myself arrived in Geneva, we found that we were not Liberals, Tories or Independents-we were Canadians. The treatment accorded to us by the members of the governing party was all that it could possibly have been. Sir George Foster and myself were treated as well as if we had been Liberals- but we were not and that perhaps is something to be thankful for-and I want to say publicly that I think this government deserves credit, not because they appointed us but because they appointed those who were not of their own party, and having done that they treated us as well as though we had been of their own party.
Until I visited Geneva I was something like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), I was not a particular enthusiast for the League of Nations. I believed that it was a cumbersome machine which had in this country some advocates who tvere not very devoted to the interests of the common folks. This view led me to become skeptical of the work being done, but after my visit I have been convinced that it is accomplishing most excellent results. I would make a suggestion to this government, if they should be the government in power when the next appointments are made, that they send the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). This may seem like a drastic suggestion, but drastic action is necessary. I am sure that he would come back an enthusiast for the league. I found that those who went to scoff remained to pray.
The suggestion has been made that this trip was a joy ride, and I think it was particularly applied to me. I resent that, not because it was applied to me but because it was applied to a Canadian who was acting as a delegate to the League of Nations. If any Canadians have gone to Geneva in the past thinking of their trip as a holiday, they should be severely censured. To learn the workings of the cumbersome machinery of this parliament is not an easy task or one that can be learned rapidly, and it is more difficult to become familiar with the assembly and the committees of the League of Nations.
I would like to offer a few practical suggestions. First of all, I think the government should make the appointments as early as possible, so that those who are appointed may inform themselves on the subjects to be brought before the league. To do that takes considerable reading and time. It seems to me to be rather an insult to the greatness of the work of the league to send people who are ill-prepared. We had almost no time in which to prepare ourselves. There may have

been some who had these subjects at their finger tips, but I assure the committee that I was not in that category.
Another suggestion I would make is that the authority should not be centred in the head of the delegation. In making this suggestion I am not insinuating that the gentleman who headed the delegation was not very able or exceptionally well informed, but if the authority was diffused among the members of the delegation and each one made responsible for certain items on the agenda they would then feel a responsibility to inform themselves regarding particular items, and to discharge their duties to a degree which they cannot feel when they are not in the last analysis fully responsible. My next suggestion may amuse the committee, but I think there should be continuity in the delegation. The committee may think that I have a desire to be sent back to Geneva, but it will realize that if the members of this House of Commons were changed every year, with the exception of one or two, there would be considerable difficulty in doing even reasonably good work. New delegates are appointed each year and it is only by the time they have to depart that they are able to learn the run of things.
As Canadians, and particularly as members of this House of Commons, I think we should rid our minds of all thoughts that attending the assembly of the league is a joy ride. I would like to see the Minister of External Affairs attend the assembly of the league each year, but as he is also the Prime Minister, I realize that that would be impossible. However, someone closely attached to the Department of External Affairs and responsible to that department, such as the under secretary, should attend these meetings. Eight prime ministers and twenty ministers of external affairs attended the tenth assembly of the league.
I think that every facility should be granted to acquaint the parliament of Canada and the people of Canada with what the delegates have seen and what they have done.
I think the delegates before they leave Canada should be well acquainted with the mind of the cabinet in regard to the matters appearing upon the agenda. Another necessary qualification for this work is an understanding of the French language. I was never so sorry that I could not speak French as I was when I attended the league this year. It does seem a pity that more Canadians do not become acquainted with our two languages.

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
I make these suggestions in good faith because I feel that if they are aoted upon, the work at Geneva will be vastly improved. We have a tremendous work to do there. We are the only member of the league from the North American continent. When I realized the number of seats held by South America, and the great importance Europe attaches to itself in the work of the league, I was convinced that we have not been living up to our full responsibility to this new community, the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to express my thanks to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for drawing the attention of the house and of the country to the composition of Canada's representation at Geneva at the assembly of the league last year. He drew attention particularly to the fact that the delegation was not composed merely of members of one political party. I think the delegation represented, so far as it was possible so to do, pretty much all shades of opinion in parliament. May I say to the hon. member for Southeast Grey that the government felt that the country as a whole would appreciate there being on the representation from Canada a woman representative, and that we could think of no one who could more appropriately represent the women of Canada than the first woman member in the House of Commons? If there was ever any doubt as to the wisdom of the choice, that doubt was dispelled the moment my hon. friend accepted the invitation, attended the League of Nations and made known her impressions and views with respect to its work. The suggestions which have been made to-night by her are, I think, entirely to the point. They are all of a character that. I believe, should receive and, I may say, will be given very careful attention.
Mr. STEW"ART (Leeds):	There are two
advantages that we may expect to derive from the League of Nations and from the fact that we send representatives there. The first is the contribution which we through our representatives make to the work and the undertakings of the league. As has been suggested, it is very important that those who go there should be well equipped in every way with information in advance as to the agenda, and should be assigned some particular part in the work that is to be done. The other advantage to be derived from sending representatives to the league is the information which is brought back to us and which is disseminated amongst the Canadian people
as to the work, objects and accomplishments of the league. When we refer a matter to any committee of the house it is quite in order to expect and receive from that committee a report. While listening to the discussion I was thinking it would be to our advantage if,- when these delegates return, we had a report as to the situation as they see it from the Canadian standpoint. So far as I know no such written report has ever been made by the delegates from Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A sixty page
report was submitted to parliament more than a month ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have not seen it yet. It has not come to my mail box. That is after all the line along which we shall get the best results, namely, by making known the objects, work and accomplishments of the league and the part which our representatives have taken in its work. If such a report is available it should be given very wide distribution and should be made known to all who are interested in the work of the league.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The report was tabled and the announcement thereof appeared in the votes and proceedings. Copies were distributed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Copies may
have been distributed amongst the members, but that is not the distribution I have in mind. I have in mind a much wider distribution than that, because that, after all, will touch only the fringe of the situation and will not reach many organizations and people who are deeply interested in this work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to endorse the statement made by the hon. member for Leeds as to the interest taken in reports given by members of the delegation to Geneva on their return to Canada and the advisability of a wide distribution of those reports. It was my good fortune last year to be asked to address many meetings on this question, and I always found the people more interested in the proceedings at Geneva and the work of the League of Nations than on any other question. Wherever I had an opportunity to speak to the Canadian people on the matter, they were keenly interested in knowing how the work was conducted, about the people who came from other countries, their objects and particularly their outlook.
1396	COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
One thing that interested them more than anything else was the spirit which is evident at Geneva in the gatherings of the assembly and things of that sort. Sometimes in such conferences as that which is now proceeding in London and that which takes place annually in Geneva in the assembly and council of the league, there is apparently a great deal of talk and not so much work done. The old farm saying, "Much cry and little wool," is, in the minds of some people, applicable, but the same thing is true of every parliamentary gathering. It is unquestionably true of this house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let the hon. member speak for himself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am speaking
for myself, and I would like to associate my hon. friend with me in speaking for ourselves. This however is more apparent than real. In a gathering such as this, where men and women come from all parts of Canada and their opinions are so diverse, it is necessary to do much talking and to delay proceedings a long time until matters are threshed out. The same thing is true in committees. In Geneva the business is conducted in the same way and according to the same principle but on a much larger scale. There were many women delegates at the assembly last year-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Ten.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I thought there were more than that. There were eight or ten on the committee on which I had the pleasure of sitting. As they come from all parts of the world, represent almost all the highly civilized countries, and discuss very important affairs, it is inevitable that much time must be taken in and much thought given to the carrying on of the work of the assembly.
It is not correct to say that the assembly is a holiday in itself. Through the hot weather of the month of September in Geneva, in poorly ventilated halls with very little fresh air coming in, sitting under very difficult circumstances-which will be remedied as soon as the new parliamentary buildings are completed-the delegates stuck to their work, not from three o'clock in the afternoon but from ten o'clock in the morning and in committees for long stretches of time on end. I can assure this committee that anyone who sat in the assembly or in the committees and paid attention to the work that was being carried on certainly worked hard. The parliament of the nations that meets at Geneva

is unquestionably becoming the most important political gathering in the world. Canada gets not only the benefit of which the hon. member for Leeds spoke, that is of learning through the delegates what goes on there and how it is done, but also a good deal of benefit from the wholesome advertising she should get and has been able to get all through the years during the ten assemblies of the^ league. One of the fine things that a Canadian meets in Geneva is the high regard in which this country is held by the assembly of the league and by the men who come there year after year from the various countries. This is due I think to the class of members who have been sent there from the earliest days of the league down to the present time, with due allowance for modesty on the part of some of us who happened to be there on one occasion.
My only regret is that more members of parliament have not been able to go and that I did not know more about the league in previous years and in the session during the year in which it was my good fortune to be asked by the government to be one of the representatives at Geneva. It is well worth while to study the work of the league, to render what assistance we can by word, thought and influence in this country and to keep in touch with the work that is being carried on there. Whenever possible we should endeavour to visit Geneva and see how the work of the nations is being conducted. It is a big thing, a growing thing. The spirit that is evident at Geneva is extremely strong. I had never had an opportunity before to realize how necessary and wise it was for men and women to talk and work and keep on talking and working even when apparently they were not coming to a solution of their difficulties. I happened to be on the fifth committee, which dealt, amongst other things, with narcotics. During the first meeting of the committee the delegates of certain countries in Europe made statements that their governments had last year voluntarily instructed the manufacturers of narcotics that they must cut down their output to a certain figure. They did this voluntarily. The Canadian delegation thought that this would be a good time to introduce a resolution looking to a conference of all the manufacturing countries, with perhaps some of the victim countries, in order to secure a limitation of the manufacture of narcotics, and then ration them in order to avoid suffering on the part of those who needed them, and avoid also the contraband manufacturing of narcotics. The Canadian

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
delegation announced to the British delegation that they had this in mind. The British delegation had introducted a resolution of that character five years before, but had not succeeded in getting it passed. It was evident that the British delegation wished to reintroduce such a resolution at that time, and in cooperation with the Canadian delegation the resolution was introduced. At sitting after sitting of the committee that question was fought over. Everybody wanted to do something about it, but it was difficult to come to an agreement as to terms. The resolution was moved and many amendments were considered. At times it looked to some of the delegates from other countries that the situation was hopeless. But finally, after a drafting committee had been appointed, and had done much work, a solution was arrived at; a resolution was passed unanimously calling for a conference, to be held shortly, of all the manufacturing nations, with at least an equal number of the victim nations, in order to secure a reduction in the manufacture of narcotics and their rationing so as not to increase the price, and also to take steps to guard against what happened in this country in connection with a reduction in the manufacturing of another article, and its subsequent illicit manufacture and sale. My experience on that committee indicated the wisdom and the necessity of continued discussion with a view to reaching an amicable solution. Of course, that is not new: we do it in committees of this house all the time, and much of the important work of the League of Nations is done in committees, just as is the case in this parliament.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When we come to the next
vote we shall find an item that seems to have been overlooked by a number of those who have spoken. In addition to the publications of the League of Nations for distribution to members of parliament, we subscribe for the publications of the Empire Parliamentary Association. These reports and publications come to our letter boxes in such numbers that unless one follows them closely he is very likely to pass over them. But as the hon. member for Southeast Grey will agree, it is not difficult, if one takes advantage of what is offered just in these publications of the League of Nations and of the Empire Parliamentary Association, to keep fairly well abreast of the general current of affairs, and at least to know what is going on and what is going to be dealt with by the league in the assembly and otherwise. I think that that is money well spent. Perhaps I am a little ahead, Mr. Chairman, in discussing that vote.
We have a League of Nations society in Canada, which is doing its best to increase its membership. It has a publication called Interdependence. If the people of this country only realized it, there are publications available which will enable an3'body who chooses to take advantage of them to keep fairly well abreast of what is going on in the league. Up until the last ten years we probably took more of an academic interest in these matters because we were a little far afield, but since the war we have been drawn more into the current of events and we feel somewhat of the interest the Britisher is bound to have every day he reads of foreign affairs in his morning paper. I do not think that the press in Canada up to the last two or three years have carried items of foreign news to any great extent and it is not to be wondered at that the people of Canada have not felt bound to take a great deal of interest in foreign affairs. But the great war brought us into the swirl of events, and as time goes on we shall be drawn farther afield than we have been up to this time.
I	am very glad to have heard what my hon. friend from Southeast Grey has said about the league and her experiences there. 1 should like to say that that is no different from any other trip. If one wants to work, one works; and if one wants to make a joyride of it, one can do so. The League of Nations being of the importance it is, and Canada taking part in it to the great extent it does, I would not for a moment consider cutting down our activities in that regard, but rather I think we should seek to further our connection with the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish to say a word or two on a question not dealing with the league at all, but dealing with external affairs. It is of some importance, and perhaps may be said on this item as well as on any other.
There is an organization called the Parliamentary Economic Conference which, except for the interval of the war, has been meeting yearly for the past twenty or twenty-five years. Last fall it met in Berlin, Germany, and some sixty-two or sixty-three countries were represented. The majority of the representatives pay their own expenses. I am not suggesting that this is an opportunity for this government or any government to spend more money. I am pointing out that it is an economic conference of a good deal of importance, attended by some sixty-two countries. At the last meeting Great Britain had some twenty-five representatives. Canada had no representative present; at least, she would not have had a representative had not a member of this house of parliament been in

Supply-External Affairs-Geneva
London at that time and been asked by Sir Howard d'Egville, the secretary of the Empire Parliamentary Association, to represent Canada. He hesitated to go, pointing out that he was not even a supporter of the government, but it was represented to him that this was a parliamentary organization that had nothing to do with governments and was not political in any way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who was the representative?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Was not the Minister of National Revenue present at that conference?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, there was no other representative of Canada present, and I went only incidentally. I had not intended to mention my name until the Prime Minister asked for it.
The Parliamentary Economic Conference is a business organization dealing, for instance, with such subjects as the rationalization of industry and matters of that kind. It covers a large field. It is an organization which should be attended by business men, and I am sure that we have in this country outstanding business men who would be glad to represent Canada at the annual meeting of that conference. It is, I think, of some importance. I do not know that it would be of any great value, except that it would have its value in contacts and in a certain amount of advertising for our country, so many countries being represented at the conference. As I said, Great Britain had twenty-five delegates, and there were also representatives from Japan and various otheT countries. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that it might be well for the Department of External Affairs to get in touch with Sir Howard d'Egville and see if Canada cannot be represented at future conferences, not at the expense of this country at all, but by prominent business men of Canada who would be glad to attend at their own expense. Most of the representatives of Great Britain went at their own expense. While some of the countries pay the expenses of their delegates, I think the majority do not. I offer that suggestion for the consideration of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

iMr. WOODSWORTH: Before we pass from external affairs, although it does not come directly under this item, would the Prime Minister give us a statement with regard to our present relationship to Russia? How far have we established connections now that relations have been established between Great Britain and Russia? To be more specific, if, for example, a Canadian wishes to go to Russia can he obtain a passport here, or must he obtain it through the British authorities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
So far as
relations between Canada and Russia are concerned, they are similar to those existing between Canada and any other country, other than those in which we have legations. We have legations only in the United States, France, and Japan; we have not legations, in nor do we receive diplomatic representatives from, any other countries than those three. Russia in that regard is in exactly the same relationship to Canada as, say, Italy or Austria or Germany.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Did we not break
our relationship with Russia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MB. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: There had been a special diplomatic privilege given to Russia. That was discontinued. Russia at that time under a special treaty negotiated with Great Britain to which this country had become a party, had a position of advantage, diplomatically, relative to that granted to any other country. A change was made in that regard, as my hon. friend knows, when the treaty was abrogated. That, however, has left Russia, so far as receiving diplomatic missions by Canada is concerned, simply in the same position as any other country, save the three 1 have mentioned. If any one from Canada wishes to visit Russia he can obtain a passport from the passport office at Ottawa. To admit him to Russia, it would have to be vised, I believe, by Russian authorities.

speechtext:
Regarding this
particular item, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. McLean) suggested there should be
a wider distribution of literature with respect to the league. I know of no way in which it can be done more effectively than by the League of Nations Society. Ordinary membership of the society costs only a dollar a year, but that does not pay the expenses incident to distributing the bulletins and other papers sent out to the ordinary members. The more help the government gives to the society the more they will be able to distribute this literature to their ordinary members. That is the cheapest and simplest way of securing that distribution.
